newsitem.title: USA: Oil companies agree to end alleged conspiracy.
newsitem.headline: Oil companies agree to end alleged conspiracy.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Justice said Friday it won agreement from three oil companies to stop conspiring to reduce broker charges, though the oil firms denied or down-played any wrongdoing.

The Justice Department said in a statement that the settlement meant "the three colluding firms -- AIG Trading Corp., BP Exploration & Oil Inc. and Cargill International S.A. -- will no longer be able to conspire to reduce broker commissions."

The four-year-old investigation was into allegations that the three firms, and unnamed "others," conspired by telephone and via meetings in Europe and the United States to share information with the purpose of pushing down the fees brokers charged for arranging deals on North Sea Brent oil contracts.
The settlement is subject to agreement by the U.S. District Court for the Southern District in Manhattan.
"BP strongly denies that it engaged in any improper conduct," said Tom Koch, a BP spokesman in New York.

"We see the consent order as a satisfactory conclusion to this lengthy investigation," Koch added. "BP has always made its decisions about the commission rates it will pay for trades unilaterally and will continue to do so in the future."

A spokesman for parent American International Group Inc. said: "AIG Trading Corp. cooperated fully with the Department of Justice and is pleased that the matter has been resolved without any monetary payment."
Cargill Inc. in Minneapolis, parent of Cargill International, said the company had no comment on the settlement.

Gina Talamona, a spokesperson for the Justice department, said the settlement represented no compromise on the part of the department. Rather, she said securing a court order to bar them from any further collusion was the objective.
"It is far from saying a case was dropped," Talamona said. "They agreed they will no longer get together to do this so that resolved our concerns."
The collusion is alleged to have been over forward-delivery contracts for Brent crude, the world benchmark for oil prices.

The murky market for Brent, which has a direct influence on prices for more than half the world's daily oil trade, is often the subject of price manipulation charges and was investigated by British authories about three years ago, though without any charges being brought.
